definition.text: A conservation land trust is a nonprofit that buys and looks after land, or holds conservation easements on it, to protect nature, farmland or recreation.

facts.text: It may own land outright or buy an easement or development, mining or logging rights while the land stays private.
Land trusts rely on donations, grants and public programmes; landowners often donate easements or land itself.
Many depend on volunteers: in the 2005 US census, 54% of land trusts were all-volunteer.
The first, the Trustees of Reservations in Massachusetts, was founded in 1891; by 2021 the US had over 1,300.
Most work regionally, though global ones include The Nature Conservancy and the World Land Trust.
Local and regional US trusts protected almost 9.4 million acres by 2003, double the 1998 figure.

definition.text: Environmental finance is a branch of finance that uses market-based environmental policy tools, such as pricing and trading schemes, to make investment less harmful to nature.

facts.text: It seeks to move business resources toward sustainable investments while keeping profits.
Richard Sandor proposed a course on emission markets in 1992 at the University of Chicago, later called Environmental Finance.
Inspired by the idea of social cost, Sandor focused on cap-and-trade along with taxes and subsidies.
Under cap-and-trade, a total emissions cap is set and firms receive permits they can buy or sell, rewarding cuts and penalising excess.
The Dow Jones Sustainability Index, launched in 1999, rates the ecological and social impact of stocks for investors.
Climate finance, a part of it, splits into mitigation finance, which cuts emissions, and adaptation finance; mitigation takes over 90% of climate spending.

definition.text: Official development assistance is the OECD's measure of foreign aid: money that rich countries' governments give to promote poorer countries' development and welfare.

facts.text: The OECD Development Assistance Committee adopted the concept in 1969.
Most is grants, but soft loans count if their grant element is at least 25%.
ODA was US$168 billion in 2019, of which US$152 billion came from DAC donors.
In 2019, 28% of all ODA was multilateral, pooled through bodies such as the EU, the World Bank's IDA and UN agencies.
In 2025 aid from DAC donors fell 23% after inflation, the biggest yearly drop on record.
Critics call it an untidy, somewhat arbitrary category that counts spending mainly benefiting donors, such as refugee costs at home.
It is a channel for international public conservation finance, through grants, concessional loans and technical help.

definition.text: The best-known aid target says rich countries should give 0.7% of their national income as official development assistance.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly formalised it on 24 October 1970; Sweden and the Netherlands first met it in 1974, and few others have since.
DAC donors as a group have given around 0.3-0.35% of their income since the 1970s.
In 2019 six countries met the target, and the UK cut its aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of income in 2021.

title: Tied aid

definition.text: Tied aid is aid given on condition that the money is spent on goods from the donor country or a small group of countries.

facts.text: Its legitimacy has long been disputed within the OECD's aid committee, which has set targets to reduce it.
A review found that in 2009, 51% of contract value was spent in donor countries though donors reported only 14% of aid as tied.

contested_note: Donors have long disputed whether tying aid to their own exports is legitimate.
